sections.h2: What a small estate affidavit is
sections.html:
It is a sworn statement that lets a person holding a dead person's money or property release it to the heirs without a court case. Section 25-1 of the Probate Act of 1975, 755 ILCS 5/25-1, tells a bank, a transfer agent or anyone owing the decedent money to pay or deliver to the people named in a conforming affidavit. A holder who acts in good faith on a copy that substantially follows the statutory form is protected as if the payment had gone to a court appointed representative.

For homeowners, the phrase that counts is "personal property." The affidavit covers cash, accounts, safe deposit contents and similar items. It does not cover the house.

sections.h2: The Illinois small estate affidavit limit
sections.html:
The limit is $150,000 in tangible and intangible personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State. That figure comes from Public Act 104-346, effective August 15, 2025, and applies to a decedent who died on or after that date. A second amendment, Public Act 104-624, takes effect January 1, 2027. It leaves the $150,000 figure alone while listing vehicle types that no longer count as excluded vehicles.

P.A. 104-624January 1, 2027$150,000Living quarters vehicles, motor homes, mini motor homes, van campers, non self propelled vehicles, commercial vehicles, implements of husbandry, buses and commuter vans are not excluded

If the affidavit is used only to retitle vehicles with the Secretary of State, it can transfer them regardless of the value of the personal estate.

sections.h2: Can the affidavit transfer a house?
sections.html:
No. The statute covers transferring personal property, and Illinois Legal Aid Online is plain that the affidavit can't move real property such as a house. The decedent's real estate may already have moved by a Transfer on Death Instrument or by joint tenancy. In that case the affidavit can still handle the rest of the estate.

When the house is titled in the decedent's name alone, the usual route runs through the circuit court. Under 755 ILCS 5/20-1, a court appointed representative takes possession of the decedent's real estate during administration, collects rents, keeps the buildings in repair, pays taxes and liens and may insure the property. Subsection (d) leaves intact the representative's power to sell or mortgage real estate under the Probate Act.

Subsection (a-5) sets two gates. No letters of office can be outstanding on the estate, and no petition for letters can be contemplated or pending in Illinois or any other jurisdiction. The decedent's personal estate, whether it passes by intestacy or under a will, must stay within the dollar limit. The affiant also attaches a copy of the death certificate, and a certified copy of the will if one was filed.

Whoever holds a will must file it with the clerk of the proper county right after the testator dies (755 ILCS 5/6-1). Hiding a will for 30 days after learning of the death is a Class 3 felony. The affidavit is signed before a notary under penalty of perjury, and an out of state affiant names an Illinois agent for service of process.

The form can be downloaded from the Secretary of State's website or picked up at the circuit clerk's office. Make at least two copies of the signed affidavit to show each bank or company holding property of the estate. A holder who refuses to turn the property over can be taken to civil court.

Items the affidavit must list include:

  • The affiant's addresses and relationship to the decedent
  • The decedent's name, date of death and last residence
  • Each asset with its fair market value and every registered vehicle
  • Known unpaid debts by class, or a statement that all debts were paid
  • The surviving spouse, minor children and adult dependent children
  • The heirs or legatees and each share

Creditors come before heirs. Paragraph 7.5 of the affidavit requires every valid claim to be paid from the estate before anything goes to an heir or legatee, and if a class can't be paid in full, its claims are paid pro rata. The affiant also agrees to indemnify creditors, heirs and anyone relying on the affidavit for losses caused by the affiant's act or omission, with attorney's fees owed to a person who recovers.

The statutory order of classes is:

  • Class 1: funeral and burial expenses, administration expenses and statutory custodial claims
  • Class 2: the surviving spouse's or child's award
  • Class 3: debts due the United States
  • Class 4: wages owed employees, up to $800 per claimant, for services within 4 months before death, and last illness expenses
  • Class 5: money or property held in trust that cannot be identified or traced
  • Class 6: debts due the State of Illinois and local governments in Illinois
  • Class 7: all other claims

The award for a surviving spouse who was an Illinois resident is $20,000 plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at the time of death. With no spouse, the same amount goes to those children in equal shares.

sections.h2: Selling an inherited home when the affidavit doesn't apply
sections.html:
The seller needs legal authority first. If the home is in the decedent's name alone, an heir can't sign a deed on the strength of an affidavit, so the sale waits for a court appointed representative or another transfer of title. Ask the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the decedent lived what filings the probate division requires, and ask the county recorder what proof of authority it wants with a deed.

Under section 20-1, a representative may not take possession of the part of the real estate that an heir or legatee occupies as a residence unless the will says so or the court finds possession is necessary for claims, administration costs, taxes, preservation or distribution. On petition, the court may also hand possession to an heir or legatee if the property won't be needed to pay debts.

The affidavit can still handle bank accounts and vehicles while the house moves through probate, which keeps the two tracks separate. Taxes, insurance and upkeep on the house go on in the meantime, and the representative carries those duties.

sections.h2: What to bring to the lawyer or clerk
sections.html: Before you meet the lawyer or visit the circuit clerk, collect the death certificate, the deed, the latest tax bill, any will and a list of the accounts and vehicles. Those papers let them tell you quickly whether the affidavit fits, whether the house needs a court case, and how long each path is likely to take. A cash buyer can usually close once someone with authority can sign, so the paperwork on your side sets the pace.

faqs.q: What is the small estate limit in Illinois?
faqs.a: $150,000 in personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State, under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 as amended by Public Act 104-346.

faqs.q: Can I sell my parent's house with a small estate affidavit?
faqs.a: No. The affidavit transfers personal property only. A house titled in the decedent's name usually needs a court appointed representative before it can be sold, unless it already passed by a Transfer on Death Instrument or joint tenancy.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay the decedent's debts before giving heirs their share?
faqs.a: Yes. The affiant must pay valid claims in the statutory order before any distribution to an heir or legatee, and signs an indemnity for losses caused by the affiant's acts or omissions.

faqs.q: How much is the spouse or child award in an Illinois small estate?
faqs.a: $20,000 for the surviving spouse plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at death. With no spouse, that sum is divided equally among the children.

faqs.q: Does a small estate affidavit need a notary?
faqs.a: Yes. The form is signed and sworn before a notary public under penalty of perjury, and a fraudulent statement is perjury under section 32-2 of the Criminal Code of 2012.
